IRD20 · Pathology · Study Guide

Derm Neoplastic Diseases

Learning objectives

  1. LO 1Name what drives the major skin cancers, explain how skin phototype (Fitzpatrick I–VI) changes a person's risk, and describe how BCC, SCC and melanoma tend to look and behave in lighter versus darker skin.
  2. LO 2For basal cell carcinoma: recognize its main clinical forms, explain its risk factors and hedgehog-pathway biology (including inherited Gorlin syndrome), identify it at the bedside and under the microscope, and explain why it destroys locally but rarely spreads and how each form is treated.
  3. LO 3Follow the squamous pathway from actinic keratosis to SCC in situ to invasive SCC (clinical look and histology), explain the risk factors and UV/p53 biology, describe the keratoacanthoma and verrucous carcinoma variants, and summarize how SCC behaves and is treated.
  4. LO 4For melanoma: list the risk factors and driver genes, compare the superficial spreading, nodular, lentigo maligna, acral lentiginous and amelanotic forms by how common they are, where they occur and how they grow, and use ABCDE to judge a pigmented lesion.
  5. LO 5Recognize melanoma under the microscope, explain how Breslow thickness is measured and why it matters most, list the other prognostic factors, and outline management from excision and sentinel node biopsy to systemic therapy.

MAPBig picture

  • UV × skin phototype → biggest risk factor for every skin cancer
    • Fitzpatrick I–II (always sunburn) = highest risk
    • Skin of color → non-UV drivers (HPV, scars, immunosuppression) → later diagnosis
  • BCC = most common → hedgehog (PTCH1 loss / SMO gain) → pearly, local destruction, ~never metastasizes
    • Nodular · superficial · morpheaform → Mohs / excision / conservative / vismodegib
  • SCC = 2nd most common → chronic UV + HPV + smoking + immunosuppression → p53, thymine dimers
    • AK (partial) → SCC in situ (full, BM intact) → invasive (keratin pearls)
    • Variants: keratoacanthoma · verrucous carcinoma
  • Melanoma = >90% of skin cancer deaths → MAPK (BRAF V600E), CDKN2A familial
    • SSM (radial → vertical) · nodular (vertical only) · LMM (old face) · ALM (palms/soles/nails) · amelanotic
    • ABCDE to find it
  • Breslow depth = #1 prognostic factor → T stage (+ ulceration) → margins, SLNB (T1b+), checkpoint/BRAF-MEK therapy

LO 1Causes of skin cancer, skin phototype and skin toneWhy lighter skin gets more cancer, and why darker skin gets diagnosed later

By the end: you can rank the three skin cancers by frequency and deadliness, fill in the Fitzpatrick scale, mark which risk factors favor SCC vs BCC, and predict how each cancer presents in lighter vs darker skin.
Q1. What are the big three skin cancers, and how common and how deadly is each?
  • ~1 in 5 Americans will develop a skin cancer.
  • Non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC) = BCC + SCC → ~3 million Americans/year.
    • Basal cell carcinoma → most common skin cancer (and the most common cancer overall).
    • Squamous cell carcinoma → 2nd most common overall; most common in African Americans.
  • Melanoma → far less common but causes >90% of skin cancer–related deaths; invasive melanoma is projected to be the 5th most commonly diagnosed cancer in men and women.

BCC

Most common → rarely kills (local destruction)

SCC

2nd overall · #1 in Black patients → metastasizes <5%

Melanoma

Least common of the three → most deaths

CheckWhich skin cancer is most common, and which causes the most deaths?
BCC is most common; melanoma causes >90% of skin cancer deaths.
Q2. What is the single biggest risk factor, and what is the Fitzpatrick scale?
  • Skin phenotype is the biggest risk factor for skin cancer → it sets how susceptible the skin is to UV radiation.
  • Skin type (how fair the skin is) is a risk factor for all types of skin cancer — BCC, SCC and melanoma.
  • The Fitzpatrick scale grades skin by how it reacts to UV (sunburn vs tan):
TypeSkin colorResponse to UVSkin cancer risk
IWhiteAlways sunburns, never tansHighest (BCC, SCC, UV-type melanoma)
IIWhiteSunburns easily, tans with difficulty
IIIBeigeMild sunburn, tans graduallyIntermediate
IVBrownRarely sunburns, tans easily
VDark brownVery rarely sunburns, tans very easilyLowest UV risk → but later diagnosis, non-UV drivers
VIBlackNever sunburns, tans very easily
CheckA patient says she "I always sunburn and never tan." Fitzpatrick type?
Type I → highest UV-driven skin cancer risk.
Q3. Which etiologies matter for which non-melanoma cancer?
  • UV radiation → main driver of both BCC and SCC (but the pattern differs).
  • HPV and cigarette smoking → especially SCC.
  • Higher-risk patients → more frequent skin screening.
Risk factorSCCBCC
UV exposure+ chronic, cumulative+ intermittent, intense (sunburns)
Ionizing radiation++
HPV+ (genitals, nails)±
Cigarette smoking+—
Chronic non-healing wounds / scars+ (Marjolin ulcer)—
Organ transplant (immunosuppression)+ (~100×)+ (~6×)
Basal cell nevus syndrome—+
Xeroderma pigmentosum++
  • Transplant recipients (chronic immunosuppression): SCC risk ↑ ~100-fold, Merkel cell ~24-fold, BCC ~6-fold, melanoma ~2-fold → immune surveillance normally clears UV- and HPV-damaged keratinocytes.
  • HPV → E6 degrades p53, E7 binds Rb → same mechanism as cervical SCC; HPV causes SCC in skin too, not only the cervix.
CheckName two risk factors that push you toward SCC rather than BCC.
Any two of: smoking, organ transplant/immunosuppression, HPV, chronic wounds/scars, chronic cumulative UV.
Step 1 HY
  • Xeroderma pigmentosum: autosomal recessive defect in nucleotide excision repair → cannot remove UV pyrimidine dimers → SCC, BCC and melanoma in childhood.
  • In transplant patients the usual BCC > SCC ratio reverses → SCC dominates and is more aggressive.
  • Arsenic exposure → SCC.
Step 1 trap

"Darker skin = no skin cancer" is wrong. Risk from UV is lower, but cancers arise at non-sun-exposed sites (palms, soles, nails, genitals, scars) and are found later → worse outcomes.

Memory tool

SCC "HITS" hard: HPV, Immunosuppression, Tobacco, Scars (Marjolin) — on top of chronic sun.

Q4. How do the big three differ between lighter and darker skin tones?
  • Lighter skin → strong UV association → sun-exposed sites; incidence much higher (especially NMSC, above all BCC).
  • Skin of color → cancer is less associated with UV → drivers are chronic wounds, immune suppression and HPV; often diagnosed at later stages → do thorough full-skin exams (palms, soles, nails, genitals).
CancerLighter skin tonesDarker skin tones
BCCMost common skin cancer; pearly, translucent; sun-exposed sitesLess common; often pigmented → mimics melanoma
SCCRough, scaly lesions on sun-exposed skinMost common skin cancer; often driven by HPV or chronic inflammation/scars; can be pigmented
MelanomaUV-associated types that spread superficially (superficial spreading)Usually not UV-associated; check palms, soles, nails (acral lentiginous); diagnosed later
CheckMost common skin cancer in African Americans?
Squamous cell carcinoma (often at non-sun-exposed sites, with poorer prognosis from etiology and late diagnosis).
Buzzwords
"always sunburns, never tans" → Fitzpatrick I "kidney transplant + scaly nodules" → SCC "child with many skin cancers, photosensitive" → xeroderma pigmentosum "dark patch on the sole of a Black patient" → acral lentiginous melanoma
Step 1 trap

Pigment ≠ melanoma. BCC (pigmented BCC) and SCC can both be pigmented, especially in darker skin → biopsy decides.

ApplyLO 1 application questions

A1A 55-year-old man 8 years after kidney transplant has several crusted nodules on his scalp and hands. Which skin cancer has risen most, and roughly how much?
SCC, ~100-fold. Immunosuppression removes immune surveillance of UV/HPV-damaged keratinocytes; BCC rises only ~6-fold.
A2A Black woman has an enlarging ulcer within a 30-year-old burn scar on her shin. What cancer and what drives it?
SCC arising in a scar (Marjolin ulcer). In skin of color SCC is the most common skin cancer and is driven by chronic inflammation/wounds, not UV.
A3A 9-year-old with severe photosensitivity, freckling and already two skin cancers. Which DNA repair pathway is defective?
Nucleotide excision repair (xeroderma pigmentosum). UV pyrimidine dimers cannot be removed → childhood BCC, SCC and melanoma.
A4Why do skin cancers in patients of color carry a worse prognosis even though incidence is lower?
Later diagnosis. They arise at sites not routinely examined and look less "classic" → found at advanced stage.

LO 2Basal cell carcinomaHedgehog pathway, three clinical subtypes, palisading + clefting, local destruction without spread

By the end: you can draw the hedgehog pathway and point to the BCC mutation and drug target, tell nodular / superficial / morpheaform apart, describe the histology, explain why BCC rarely metastasizes, and match each presentation to treatment.
Q1. Where does BCC come from, and how does it behave?
  • Most common skin cancer. Derived from undifferentiated pluripotent epithelial stem cells (basal layer and hair follicle).
  • ~80% on the head and neck.
  • Indolent → local invasion and destruction (nose, eyelid, ear).
    • Genomic stability + high stromal dependence (tumor can't survive away from its own stroma) → unlikely to metastasize (almost never).
    • High morbidity, low mortality → but a high cost burden (so many lesions to treat).
  • Risk factors:
    • Intermittent, intense sun exposure → sunburns; also ionizing radiation.
    • History of prior BCC → 44% develop another within 3 years.
CheckGive the two reasons BCC almost never metastasizes.
Genomic stability and high stromal dependence.
Q2. What goes wrong in the hedgehog pathway?
1 · PTCHinhibits SMO (brake on)
→
2 · SHH binds PTCHinhibition released → SMO active
→
3 · GLI ↑transcription factor upregulated
→
4 · Growth ↑increased cellular proliferation
  • BCC = constitutive activation of this pathway:
    • Inactivating PTCH1 mutation → tumor suppressor lost → the most important BCC mutation ("inactive Patched").
    • Activating SMO mutation → proto-oncogene stuck on.
    • TP53 mutation can also occur (more characteristic of SCC).
  • Either way: inactive Patched → overactive Smoothened → GLI → growth.
CheckPTCH1: tumor suppressor or oncogene? And which protein does vismodegib block?
PTCH1 = tumor suppressor (loss-of-function). Vismodegib blocks Smoothened (SMO).
Q3. What is basal cell nevus (Gorlin) syndrome, and is it a BCC subtype?
  • Autosomal dominant, inactivating germline PTCH1 mutation → numerous BCCs starting young.
  • NOT a subtype of BCC → a genetic predisposition; patients can develop any BCC subtype.
  • Treated with vismodegib (hedgehog inhibitor).
  • Their BCCs can look like melanocytic nevi or skin tags → easily missed.
  • Two-hit logic: every cell already carries one bad PTCH1 allele → only one somatic "second hit" per cell → dozens of tumors early. Sporadic BCC needs two somatic hits → older adults, single tumors.

Gorlin major features

  • Multiple early BCCs
  • Palmoplantar pits
  • Odontogenic keratocysts of the jaw
  • Calcified falx cerebri
  • Medulloblastoma (early childhood)
  • First-degree relative affected

Minor: bifid ribs, cleft lip/palate, macrocephaly with frontal bossing, ovarian/cardiac fibromas.

CheckA 19-year-old has dozens of "moles" on the trunk; biopsies show BCC. Gene?
Germline PTCH1 (Gorlin, autosomal dominant).
Step 1 HY
  • Gorlin = BCCs + jaw keratocysts + palmar pits + falx calcification + medulloblastoma.
  • Vismodegib / sonidegib = SMO inhibitors for advanced BCC; teratogenic.
  • Hedgehog also patterns the neural tube and limbs (SHH from the zone of polarizing activity) → loss = holoprosencephaly.
Step 1 trap

The drug targets SMO, not PTCH. PTCH is a lost brake — you can't "inhibit" something already gone. Also: Gorlin is a syndrome, not a fourth clinical subtype.

Memory tool

PTCH = Parking brake; SMO = gas pedal; GLI = Go. BCC: brake cut (PTCH1) or pedal jammed (SMO). Vismo-degib takes your foot off SMO.

Q4. How do the three clinical subtypes look?
SubtypeWho / how commonFavored siteLook
NodularMost common (~50%)Face, especially noseShiny, pearly papule/nodule · arborizing vessels · ± ulceration → "rolled border" · ± pigment
SuperficialYounger patientsTrunk and extremitiesWell-circumscribed red thin plaque · subtle rolled border · ± scale/crust (microulceration) · ± pigment · mimics inflammatory dermatoses · subclinical lateral spread (skip areas)
Morpheaform (sclerosing)Less common; difficult to diagnoseFaceWhite-pink atrophic, scar-like plaque · ill-defined borders · fibrotic ± induration · ± telangiectasias · most aggressive local destruction
  • Pigmented BCC = heavy melanin in a nodular or superficial BCC (very uncommon in morpheaform) → mimics melanoma, but still shiny/pearly and often ulcerated; more common in darker skin.
CheckA red, thin, slightly scaly plaque on the back of a 40-year-old didn't improve with eczema cream. Which BCC subtype?
Superficial BCC → trunk, younger patient, mimics inflammatory dermatoses.
Buzzwords
"pearly papule, rolled borders, telangiectasias" → nodular BCC "scar-like plaque, no prior injury" → morpheaform BCC "eczema that won't heal on the trunk" → superficial BCC "upper lip lesion" → BCC
Step 1 HY

BCC above the upper lip, SCC below the lower lip. Boards phrase BCC as a "pink pearly papule with rolled borders and central ulceration" on the face of an older fair-skinned patient.

Step 1 trap

Pigmented BCC vs melanoma: a pearly sheen + ulceration favors BCC. Amelanotic melanoma is the reverse look-alike (pink bump that turns out to be melanoma).

Q5. What does BCC look like under the microscope?
  • Basaloid (blue) neoplasm connected to the epidermis.
  • Uniform cells, high nuclear : cytoplasmic ratio.
  • Lobules set in fibromucinous stroma (mucin).
  • Peripheral palisading → outer nuclei line up like fence posts.
  • Clefting / retraction → artifactual space between tumor lobule and stroma.
  • Many histologic subtypes exist (low yield — don't memorize them).
CheckBlue lobules + palisading + clefting. Which tumor? What would the pink-lobule look-alike be?
BCC. Pink (eosinophilic) keratinizing lobules with keratin pearls = SCC.
Q6. How is BCC treated?

Treatment depends on clinical/histologic subtype and location.

ScenarioTreatmentWhy
Cosmetically sensitive site (face), high-risk or recurrentMohs micrographic surgeryLayer-by-layer removal, 100% of the margin examined during surgery → maximal clearance, minimal tissue loss (~99% 5-yr cure for primary BCC)
Typical lesion on the trunkSimple (elliptical) excisionTissue is plentiful
Superficial BCC on trunk/extremityConservative: cryosurgery · electrodesiccation & curettage · topical 5-FU or imiquimodThin tumor, low-risk site
Advanced / unresectable · GorlinHedgehog inhibitor (vismodegib)Blocks SMO
DrugMechanismUse hereKey toxicity
Vismodegib (sonidegib)SMO inhibitor → hedgehog offAdvanced BCC, GorlinMuscle cramps, alopecia, dysgeusia; teratogenic
Imiquimod (topical)TLR-7 agonist → local innate/T-cell immune attackSuperficial BCC, AK, LMLocal inflammation, crusting
5-Fluorouracil (topical)Pyrimidine analog → thymidylate synthase inhibitionSuperficial BCC, AK field therapyErythema, erosions
CheckBCC on the nasal tip of a 70-year-old: best surgical option?
Mohs surgery → cosmetically sensitive site, spares tissue.
Memory tool

BCC = "Bursts" of sun (intermittent sunburns); SCC = "Sustained" sun (chronic, cumulative).

Step 1 HY

Imiquimod is the classic Step 1 TLR-7 agonist; also used for genital warts. 5-FU's systemic form is the classic thymidylate synthase inhibitor (rescue with uridine, not leucovorin).

ApplyLO 2 application questions

A1A 66-year-old had a nodular BCC excised from his nose last year. What is his risk of another, and what follow-up is needed?
~44% within 3 years. Prior BCC is itself a major risk factor → regular full-skin exams + sun protection.
A2A child with Gorlin syndrome develops dozens of BCCs; his grandmother had one BCC at 80. Explain the difference.
Two-hit hypothesis. Germline PTCH1 loss means one somatic hit per cell suffices; sporadic BCC needs two hits in the same cell (decades of UV).
A3A 34-year-old has a 1.5-cm thin red plaque with a thread-like border on the upper back, biopsy-proven BCC. Non-surgical options?
Cryosurgery, electrodesiccation & curettage, or topical imiquimod/5-FU. Superficial BCC on the trunk can be managed conservatively.
A4A locally advanced BCC around the orbit cannot be resected. Which oral drug and target?
Vismodegib → Smoothened. Shuts off GLI-driven growth despite PTCH1 loss.
A5Why is morpheaform BCC so often incompletely excised?
Ill-defined, infiltrative, scar-like borders hide its true extent → Mohs (full margin check) is preferred.

LO 3Actinic keratosis → SCC in situ → invasive SCCThree progressive stages, two special variants (keratoacanthoma, verrucous carcinoma)

By the end: you can define AK and SCC in situ by how much of the epidermis is atypical, list SCC risk factors and high-risk sites, explain UV signature mutations and p53, describe keratoacanthoma and verrucous carcinoma, and choose treatment.
Q1. Who gets cutaneous SCC, and where?
  • 2nd most common skin cancer overall; most common in African Americans → non-sun-exposed sites (do thorough exams), poorer prognosis from etiology and late diagnosis.
  • UV exposure = biggest risk factor overall (lighter skin types).
  • HPV → especially genitals and nails (screen these areas).
  • Chronic inflammation and wounds → Marjolin ulcer.
  • Smoking and immune suppression (AIDS, transplant) → key in-house risk factors.
  • High-risk sites: lips, ears, anogenital region (plus scars, mucosa).
Q2. How does UV cause SCC at the DNA level?
UVB (~300 nm)chronic, repeated exposure
→
UV signaturecyclobutane-pyrimidine dimers (thymine–thymine most common) · 6,4-photoproducts · ROS damage
→
P53 dysregulationan early event
→
No repair, no apoptosismutant keratinocytes expand → AK → SCC
  • Cutaneous SCC is more indolent than SCC elsewhere → metastasis <5% (but more than BCC).
CheckMost common UV dimer, and which gene is hit early in SCC?
Thymine–thymine cyclobutane dimer; TP53.
Step 1 HY
  • Pyrimidine dimers are fixed by nucleotide excision repair (endonuclease cuts on both sides) → defective in XP.
  • UVB = Burn (DNA damage, cancer); UVA = Aging (tanning, photoaging).
Memory tool

"T-T = Tan-Tan." UV glues two neighboring thymines together → p53 is the first guard to fall.

Q3. What separates actinic keratosis, SCC in situ and invasive SCC?
StageAtypiaClinical lookKey facts
Actinic keratosisPartial-thickness epidermal atypia (lower layers) + parakeratotic scaleRough, erythematous papule with overlying scale → sandpaper / "gritty" texture; sun-exposed, lighter skin; occasionally tenderPrecursor, NOT a subtype of SCC; <1 in 1000/yr progress; among the most common derm lesions
SCC in situFull-thickness atypia, pleomorphism, necrotic cells; basement membrane intactScaly red papule/plaque; mimics inflammatory conditionsFrom AK or de novo (Bowen disease); treated like SCC
Invasive SCCAtypical keratinocytes through the BM → pink eosinophilic lobules with keratin pearls in dermisProtean: slow or rapid; nodule, ulcer, crust; can be pigmentedHigh-risk sites: scar, lip, ear, mucosa; nerve symptoms → perineural invasion
CheckFull-thickness atypia, BM intact. Can it metastasize yet?
No → SCC in situ; no access to lymphatics/vessels until it breaches the BM. Still treated like SCC because it can progress.
Q4. How are AKs treated, and what are the special in-situ variants?

Actinic keratosis treatment

  • Single lesions → cryotherapy
  • Extensive disease → field therapy: topical imiquimod or 5-fluorouracil, or photodynamic therapy (treats subclinical lesions too)
  • Hypertrophic AK = thick, horn-like variant
  • Actinic cheilitis = AK of the lip; the lower lip is a high-risk site

SCC in situ variants

  • Bowen disease = de novo SCCIS; sun-exposed sites in older patients, sun-protected sites in younger
  • Bowenoid papulosis = genital papules from HPV-16/18
  • Erythroplasia of Queyrat = SCCIS of the penis (red, velvety glans plaque), unknown cause
CheckA bald 70-year-old has dozens of gritty papules across the scalp. Freeze each one?
No → field therapy (5-FU, imiquimod or photodynamic therapy).
Step 1 trap
  • AK vs seborrheic keratosis: AK = rough, red, gritty, sun-exposed, premalignant. SK = waxy "stuck-on" brown plaque, benign (sudden eruption of many SKs = Leser-Trélat → GI adenocarcinoma).
  • A "rash" that won't respond to steroids → biopsy for Bowen disease or superficial BCC.
Buzzwords
"sandpaper / gritty papule, bald scalp" → actinic keratosis "red velvety plaque on the glans" → erythroplasia of Queyrat "well-demarcated scaly red plaque, steroid-resistant" → Bowen disease
Step 1 HY

SCC risk tracks the degree of dysplasia: partial (AK) → full thickness (in situ) → invasion through BM. Same logic as cervical CIN 1→3.

Q5. How does invasive SCC present, behave and get treated?
  • Protean clinical presentation → broad differential; slow or rapid growth.
  • Pain, numbness or paresthesia in the lesion → perineural invasion.
  • Can be pigmented (especially darker skin) → pigment does not equal melanoma.
  • Histology: pink/eosinophilic lobules invading the dermis, keratin pearls (concentric keratin whorls) in well-differentiated tumors.
FeatureHigh-risk for metastasis
Thickness>2 mm (very high >6 mm)
Diameter>2 cm
LocationEar, lip, mucosa (tongue, vulva, penis)
OriginArising in a scar (burn, radiation) or Bowen disease
HistologyPoorly differentiated, perineural invasion
HostImmunosuppression
  • Treatment (per NCCN guidelines) → mostly surgical: Mohs vs simple excision; tumor board for high-risk cases; adjuvant radiation and chemotherapy for severe disease.
  • Cutaneous horn = clinical description of a keratin column → the base may be SCC (or AK/SK) → biopsy the base.
CheckAn SCC on the cheek causes tingling along the face. What does that suggest?
Perineural invasion → high-risk SCC.
Step 1 HY
  • Marjolin ulcer = SCC in a chronic burn scar/wound/sinus tract, usually >20 years after injury → aggressive.
  • SCC favors the lower lip (pipe/cigarette smokers, actinic cheilitis).
Memory tool

Color code the histo: BCC = Blue + Borders palisade; SCC = Strawberry-pink + Swirls (pearls).

Q6. What are keratoacanthoma and verrucous carcinoma?

Keratoacanthoma (KA)

Debated Pseudo-malignancy or SCC variant? → treated as SCC (looks like SCC histologically, can behave aggressively)

Rapid onset (weeks) → gradual involution (months)

Sun-exposed sites · well-circumscribed, crateriform nodule with a central keratinaceous core

Associations: Muir-Torre syndrome (Lynch variant) and BRAF inhibitors

Treatment: excision

Verrucous carcinoma

Low grade Well-differentiated SCC variant, HPV-associated

Low metastatic risk, high recurrence; locally destructive including bone → osteomyelitis

Mimics a wart/condyloma: exo- or endophytic papillomatous tumor; occurs in hard-to-treat areas (toes, genitals, mouth)

Treatment: excision vs amputation; radiation can trigger high-grade transformation → avoid

Verrucous carcinoma subtypeLocation
Epithelioma cuniculatumDistal extremity (sole, toe)
Giant condyloma (Buschke-Löwenstein)Anogenital
Oral florid papillomatosisOral cavity
CheckWhy is radiation avoided in verrucous carcinoma?
It can cause high-grade (anaplastic) transformation.
Step 1 HY
  • Muir-Torre = sebaceous neoplasms ± keratoacanthomas + Lynch visceral cancers (MSH2/MLH1 mismatch repair).
  • Vemurafenib → paradoxical MAPK activation in BRAF-wild-type (RAS-mutant) keratinocytes → KAs/SCCs; adding a MEK inhibitor reduces this.
Step 1 trap

Verrucous carcinoma is low grade with low metastatic risk — its danger is recurrence and local (bone) destruction, not distant spread. Don't call it "aggressive metastasizer."

Buzzwords
"grew over weeks, central keratin plug" → keratoacanthoma "wart on the sole that keeps recurring, bone erosion" → epithelioma cuniculatum "huge cauliflower anogenital mass" → Buschke-Löwenstein "ulcer in an old burn scar" → Marjolin ulcer (SCC)

ApplyLO 3 application questions

A1A 78-year-old retired farmer has a rough, enlarging plaque on the back of his hand. Which cancer does his exposure favor, and what should you look for nearby?
SCC; surrounding actinic keratoses. Chronic cumulative UV → AK field → SCC.
A2A 58-year-old has a sharply demarcated red velvety plaque on the glans; biopsy: full-thickness atypia, BM intact. Diagnosis?
Erythroplasia of Queyrat (SCC in situ of the penis).
A3A patient on vemurafenib for metastatic melanoma develops several fast-growing crateriform nodules. What are they and why?
Keratoacanthomas/SCC. BRAF inhibitors paradoxically activate MAPK in BRAF-wild-type keratinocytes.
A4A fungating wart-like toe tumor recurred twice and now erodes bone. Diagnosis, and should you irradiate?
Verrucous carcinoma (epithelioma cuniculatum); no. Excision/amputation; radiation risks high-grade transformation.
A5A pigmented ulcerated ankle lesion in a Black patient was presumed melanoma; biopsy shows keratin pearls. Lesson?
Pigmented SCC. SCC (and BCC) can be pigmented, especially in darker skin.

LO 4Melanoma: risk, genes, subtypes and ABCDEFrom MAPK to "backs of men, legs of women"

By the end: you can list melanoma risk factors, name the driver genes (BRAF, NRAS, KIT, CDKN2A, MC1R, BAP1), compare the five subtypes by frequency, site and growth, and apply ABCDE to a mole.
Q1. What is melanoma, and who gets it?
  • Malignancy of the melanocyte → neural crest-derived → cutaneous, mucosal, uveal or leptomeningeal.
  • Incidence rising, partly from earlier detection of thinner melanomas.
  • >90% of skin cancer deaths; unlike BCC it commonly metastasizes (nodes, lung, liver, brain, skin).
  • Vertical tumor thickness (Breslow depth) = #1 prognostic factor (LO 5).

Phenotype / genetic

  • Family history
  • Light skin, sunburns easily, red hair (MC1R)
  • DNA repair defects (XP)

Environmental

  • Intense intermittent and chronic sun
  • Tanning beds (<35 y)
  • Immunosuppression

Nevi

  • >100 nevi (~8–10×)
  • Atypical nevi (>5: ~4–6×)
  • Solar lentigines; prior melanoma

More moles — especially atypical ones — → ↑ melanoma risk, and relative risks multiply.

Q2. Which genes drive melanoma?
  • MAP kinase pathway most frequently implicated → BRAF, NRAS, KIT.
    • ~50% of melanomas carry BRAF V600E — also found in benign melanocytic nevi and Langerhans cell histiocytosis → the mutation alone is not enough for malignancy.
    • By melanoma group: non-CSD (intermittent sun) → BRAF-dominant, lower mutation burden; acral and mucosal → KIT prominent (can respond to imatinib).
  • CDKN2A → familial melanoma (~40%); encodes p16 (protects Rb) and p14 (protects p53); also ↑ pancreatic and lung cancer.
  • MC1R → pigmentation gene (melanocortin-1 receptor); variants → red hair, fair skin, ↑ risk.
  • BAP1-tumor predisposition syndrome → uveal melanoma, mesothelioma, renal cell carcinoma.
  • Melanomas are increasingly classified by molecular profile → guides prognosis and treatment.
CheckA melanoma family also has pancreatic cancer. Gene?
CDKN2A (p16).
Step 1 HY
  • BRAF V600E tumors: melanoma, papillary thyroid carcinoma, hairy cell leukemia, LCH, colorectal (serrated) → "BRAF V600E = Valine → glutamatE".
  • Melanoma IHC markers: S-100, HMB-45, Melan-A (MART-1), SOX10.
Step 1 trap

BRAF V600E is present in benign nevi → it is a driver, not a diagnostic test for malignancy. And BAP1 → uveal melanoma + mesothelioma (don't confuse with CDKN2A → pancreatic).

Memory tool

KIT is on your feet (acral) and in your mouth (mucosal). BAP1 = "Bad Air, Pee, 1 eye" → mesothelioma, RCC, uveal melanoma.

Q3. How do you screen a mole with ABCDE?
A · Asymmetryhalves don't match
B · Borderirregular, notched, poorly defined
C · Colorvaried within the lesion (brown, black, blue, red, white)
D · Diameter>6 mm (pencil eraser)
E · Evolvingchange in size, shape, color, symptoms
  • Evolution is the most sensitive single feature → many melanomas are <6 mm when found.
  • Suspicious lesion → excisional biopsy (full thickness, narrow margins) so depth can be measured; a superficial shave can transect the tumor.
CheckA 9-mm mole on the back, asymmetric, notched border, black/brown/gray, darkened over 6 months. Which letters? Next step?
All five → excisional biopsy.
Step 1 HY

"Ugly duckling sign": the one mole that looks different from the patient's others is suspicious. Dysplastic nevus syndrome (many atypical nevi + family history) → markedly ↑ risk.

Buzzwords
"changing mole" → melanoma until proven otherwise "pigment spilling onto the nail fold" → Hutchinson sign → acral melanoma "pink papule that biopsy calls melanocytic" → amelanotic melanoma
Q4. How do the melanoma subtypes differ?
SubtypeFrequencyTypical site / patientGrowth pattern
Superficial spreading (SSM)Most common in fair skin, 60–70%Backs of men, legs of women; de novo or in a pre-existing nevus (~50%)Slow radial → rapid vertical phase
Nodular2nd in fair skin, 15–30%Trunk, head and neckVertical only → thicker at diagnosis, worse prognosis
Lentigo maligna melanoma~10%Face (nose, cheek), 7th decade, chronic sunSlow; ~5% of LM in situ become invasive
Acral lentiginous~5% overall · up to 70% in skin of colorPalms, soles, periungual; not UV-relatedOften diagnosed at advanced stage (looks like benign lesion/trauma)
AmelanoticAny subtype can beAnywhere; no pigment → mimics BCC, broad differentialNo difference in prognosis/therapy
  • Hutchinson sign = nail pigment extending onto the proximal/lateral nail fold → suspicious for acral (subungual) melanoma.
  • Benign longitudinal melanonychia = uniform band(s) confined to the nail plate, often several nails, common in darker skin.
CheckTwo 7-mm melanomas: one SSM, one nodular. Which is worse, and why?
Nodular → vertical growth from the start → greater Breslow depth at the same diameter.
Memory tool
  • SSM = "Spreads Sideways, then Moves down".
  • Nodular = "No radial phase."
  • LMM = Lentigo on Mature (old) Mugs (face).
  • ALM = Acral → Asphalt (soles), palms, nails → skin of color.
Step 1 trap
  • Most common melanoma overall = SSM; most common in darker skin = acral lentiginous.
  • Lentigo maligna = the in situ lesion; lentigo maligna melanoma = invasive.
  • Subungual hematoma moves distally with nail growth and spares the fold; melanoma doesn't.
Step 1 HY

Boards phrase ALM as "dark lesion on the sole/under a nail in a Black or Asian patient" — not UV-related (Bob Marley died of acral melanoma of the toe).

ApplyLO 4 application questions

A1A 38-year-old with >100 atypical nevi has a mother and brother with melanoma and a grandfather who died of pancreatic cancer. Gene?
CDKN2A (p16/p14ARF). Loss of p16 frees CDK4/6 → Rb phosphorylated → G1→S unchecked.
A2A 50-year-old with uveal melanoma has a father with mesothelioma and an aunt with RCC. Syndrome?
BAP1-tumor predisposition syndrome.
A3An 80-year-old with heavily sun-damaged skin has a slowly enlarging irregular brown-black macule on the cheek. Subtype?
Lentigo maligna melanoma. Face, 7th decade+, chronic sun, slow.
A4Patient A: several uniform thin brown bands on many fingernails, folds clear. Patient B: one widening dark band with pigment on the cuticle. Which worries you?
Patient B. Single widening band + Hutchinson sign → acral lentiginous melanoma; A = benign longitudinal melanonychia.
A5A large flat irregular pigmented lesion on a man's back has spread for years and now has a raised pink nodule. What does the nodule mean?
Vertical growth phase of a superficial spreading melanoma → invasion and metastatic potential.

LO 5Melanoma histology, Breslow depth, prognosis and managementPagetoid scatter, measure in millimeters, stage by depth + ulceration

By the end: you can recognize pagetoid scatter, measure Breslow depth correctly, assign a T stage, list other prognostic factors, and outline excision margins, SLNB criteria and systemic therapy.
Q1. What does melanoma look like under the microscope?
  • Many histologic subtypes (don't memorize them) — know pagetoid scatter:
    • Single atypical melanocytes migrating upward through all levels of the epidermis (even into the stratum corneum), scattered singly.
    • Benign nevus → neat, cohesive nests along the dermal–epidermal junction that get smaller with depth (maturation).
  • Also: pleomorphism, many mitoses (including deep in the dermis), asymmetry.
CheckOrderly nests at the junction vs single cells scattered up to the granular layer. Which is melanoma?
The single scattered cells (pagetoid scatter).
Step 1 trap

"Pagetoid" spread also describes Paget disease of the breast/extramammary Paget (adenocarcinoma cells in epidermis). In a pigmented skin lesion, pagetoid single cells = melanoma.

Step 1 HY

Melanoma cells stain S-100+, HMB-45+, Melan-A+ (S-100 is shared with Schwann cells and Langerhans cells).

Q2. How is Breslow depth measured, and why is it #1?
  • Breslow depth = vertical tumor thickness in mm, from the top of the granular layer (or the ulcer base) to the deepest invasive tumor cell.
  • Thickness ≈ tumor volume → correlates with nodal and distant spread → the single most important prognostic factor for primary cutaneous melanoma.
  • T stage = Breslow depth + ulceration:
TThicknessSub-stage
TisIn situ—
T1≤1.0 mmT1a: <0.8 mm, no ulceration · T1b: <0.8 mm with ulceration or 0.8–1.0 mm
T2>1.0–2.0 mma = no ulceration · b = ulceration
T3>2.0–4.0 mma / b by ulceration
T4>4.0 mma / b by ulceration
Check0.9 mm, no ulceration. T stage?
T1b (0.8–1.0 mm counts as T1b even without ulceration).
Q3. What else predicts outcome?

Mandatory in the path report

  • Diagnosis of melanoma
  • Breslow thickness
  • Ulceration (adverse; defines "b")
  • Margins

Also reported

  • Mitotic rate
  • Subtype · associated nevus
  • Regression, tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, plasma cells
  • Vascular invasion · microscopic satellites
  • Clinical stage: nodal disease and distant metastasis → survival falls steeply from stage I to IV.
  • Diameter and color don't drive prognosis — depth does.
Step 1 trap

Clark level (anatomic layer reached) is the older system; the answer to "most important prognostic factor" is Breslow thickness (mm), not Clark level, diameter, or subtype.

Memory tool

Breslow = "Breath-depth": how deep it dives. T-stage cut points 1-2-4 mm ("one, two, four, more").

Q4. How is melanoma managed?
Excisional biopsyget Breslow depth
→
Wide excisionmargins scale with depth
→
SLNBfor T1b and deeper
→
Systemictargeted · checkpoint · chemo/radiation
→
Surveillanceclose, ≥2 years
  • Excision with appropriate margins · sentinel lymph node biopsy (T1b+) → ~20% with depth >1 mm have nodal disease.
  • Systemic therapy, chemotherapy and radiation; close surveillance for ≥2 years. Care is multidisciplinary (dermatology, pathology, surgical/medical/radiation oncology).
Tumor thicknessExcision margin
In situ0.5 cm (LM of the face may get Mohs, radiation or imiquimod)
≤1 mm1 cm
1.01–2 mm1–2 cm
>2 mm2 cm
Drug classExamplesMechanismKey toxicity
BRAF inhibitorsVemurafenib, dabrafenib, encorafenibBlock mutant BRAF V600EKA / cutaneous SCC, photosensitivity, arthralgia
MEK inhibitorsTrametinib, cobimetinib, binimetinibBlock the next MAPK step; combined with BRAF-iRash, cardiomyopathy, retinopathy; fewer KAs in combo
Anti-PD-1Nivolumab, pembrolizumabBlock T-cell PD-1 "stop" signal from tumor PD-L1Immune-related adverse events: colitis, hepatitis, thyroiditis/hypophysitis, pneumonitis, dermatitis
Anti-PD-L1(e.g., atezolizumab)Block tumor PD-L1
Anti-CTLA-4IpilimumabRemoves CTLA-4 brake on B7 costimulation → priming
Check0.6 mm, no ulceration (T1a). SLNB?
Generally no → SLNB from T1b. Wide excision with 1-cm margins + surveillance.
Step 1 HY
  • VEmuRAFenib = V600E BRAF.
  • Checkpoint inhibitors unleash T cells → autoimmunity (treat irAEs with steroids). CTLA-4 normally outcompetes CD28 for B7; PD-1 dampens effector T cells in tissue.
Buzzwords
"most important prognostic factor" → Breslow thickness "ulcerated, 0.7 mm" → T1b → SLNB "melanoma on vemurafenib, new crater nodules" → keratoacanthomas "melanoma on ipilimumab, bloody diarrhea" → immune-related colitis

ApplyLO 5 application questions

A1Forearm melanoma: Breslow 1.5 mm, no ulceration. Stage and plan?
T2a; wide excision with 1–2 cm margins + SLNB. >1 mm → ~20% nodal disease.
A2A suspicious mole is shave-biopsied superficially and the base is transected. What problem results?
Breslow depth can't be measured → staging, margins and SLNB decisions are compromised; excisional biopsy is preferred.
A3Metastatic BRAF V600E melanoma: why combine dabrafenib with trametinib instead of dabrafenib alone?
Double MAPK blockade → better, longer responses and fewer paradoxical-activation KAs/SCCs.
A4An ulcerated nodular melanoma is measured. The ulcer has removed the epidermis. Where does the measurement start?
At the ulcer base → down to the deepest invasive tumor cell; ulceration also upgrades the T sub-stage to "b".

IMGImage ID drillName the lesion before you open the card.

1 · Older patient, nose, slowly enlarging
Nodular BCC → pearly, rolled border, arborizing vessels; most common subtype.
2 · "Scar" on the nose, no injury
Morpheaform (sclerosing) BCC → ill-defined, aggressive locally → Mohs.
3 · Trunk, 40-year-old, "eczema"
Superficial BCC → thread-like rolled border (arrow), skip areas.
4 · Feels like sandpaper
Actinic keratoses → partial-thickness atypia; SCC precursor.
5 · Appeared over 4 weeks
Keratoacanthoma → rapid growth, central keratin core, involutes; treat as SCC (excise).
6 · What are the arrows?
Keratin pearls → well-differentiated SCC.
7 · Back of a man; new bump
Superficial spreading melanoma → nodule = vertical growth phase.
8 · Grew in months, uniform dark dome
Nodular melanoma → vertical only, thick at diagnosis.
9 · 80-year-old's cheek
Lentigo maligna melanoma → face, chronic sun, slow.
10 · Great toe, pigment on the fold
Acral lentiginous melanoma with Hutchinson sign.
11 · Pink papule, "probably BCC"
Amelanotic melanoma → same prognosis/therapy as pigmented.
12 · What are the arrowed cells doing?
Pagetoid scatter → melanoma.

MCQPractice questionsClick an answer to see the explanation.

Score: 0 / 0

1A 68-year-old fair-skinned man has a slowly enlarging, shiny, pearly papule on the nasal ala with fine branching surface vessels and a small central ulcer. Biopsy shows blue basaloid lobules attached to the epidermis with peripheral palisading and stromal retraction. Which molecular event most likely initiated this tumor?

C. Nodular BCC (pearly, arborizing vessels, palisading, clefting) is driven by constitutive hedgehog signaling, most importantly loss of the PTCH1 tumor suppressor. A, D, E are melanoma drivers. B describes HPV-driven SCC.

2A 74-year-old woman has a large basal cell carcinoma invading the orbit; surgery and radiation are not options. She begins an oral drug that blocks the signaling protein normally held inactive by Patched. Which drug was given?

A. Vismodegib inhibits Smoothened, shutting off GLI-driven growth in advanced BCC. B targets BRAF V600E (melanoma). C is a topical TLR-7 agonist for superficial BCC/AK. D is anti-PD-1. E inhibits KIT/BCR-ABL.

3A 17-year-old has more than 20 small skin-colored to brown papules on the face and trunk; several biopsies show basal cell carcinoma. Exam shows small pits on the palms, and a dental X-ray shows jaw cysts. His father has similar findings. Which additional tumor is this patient at increased risk for?

E. Basal cell nevus (Gorlin) syndrome: autosomal dominant germline PTCH1 loss → multiple early BCCs, palmoplantar pits, odontogenic keratocysts, falx calcification and medulloblastoma. A = CDKN2A. B and D = BAP1. C = Muir-Torre.

4A 57-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 10 years ago takes tacrolimus and mycophenolate. He has several rapidly enlarging crusted nodules on his scalp and dorsal hands. Compared with the general population, which cancer shows the greatest relative increase in his risk?

B. Chronic immunosuppression raises cutaneous SCC risk about 100-fold (vs ~6-fold BCC, ~2-fold melanoma), reversing the usual BCC > SCC ratio. C and D: melanoma risk rises only modestly. E is not linked to transplantation.

5A 71-year-old retired lifeguard has a 5-mm rough, red papule on the forehead that feels like sandpaper. Biopsy shows atypical keratinocytes confined to the lower third of the epidermis beneath a layer of parakeratosis; the basement membrane is intact. Which is the most accurate diagnosis?

D. Partial-thickness atypia with parakeratotic scale on chronically sun-exposed skin = actinic keratosis, an SCC precursor (<1 in 1000/yr progress). A requires full-thickness atypia. B requires invasion through the BM. C is a benign "stuck-on" lesion without atypia. E shows basaloid lobules with palisading.

6A 63-year-old man has had a non-healing ulcer within a burn scar on his calf for 35 years. Over 4 months it has become a raised, friable, enlarging mass. Biopsy of the mass is most likely to show which finding?

C. A Marjolin ulcer is SCC arising in a chronic scar/wound and carries a higher metastatic risk than ordinary cutaneous SCC. A = BCC. B = melanoma. D = benign wart. E = dermatofibroma/DFSP pattern.

7A 61-year-old man with metastatic melanoma began single-agent vemurafenib 2 months ago. He now has three dome-shaped nodules with central keratin-filled craters on his sun-damaged forearms, each appearing over a few weeks. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

A. BRAF inhibitors paradoxically activate MAPK signaling in BRAF-wild-type keratinocytes → rapidly growing keratoacanthomas/SCCs; adding a MEK inhibitor reduces this. B lack keratin craters. C would not have keratin cores. D is HPV-related, wart-like, slow. E are flat, scaly, not crateriform.

8A 52-year-old man has a fungating, wart-like mass on the plantar surface of his great toe that has recurred after two excisions. Imaging shows erosion into the underlying bone. Biopsy shows a well-differentiated, bulbous squamous proliferation with minimal atypia. Which statement about this tumor is most accurate?

B. Verrucous carcinoma (epithelioma cuniculatum) is a low-grade SCC variant: HPV-associated, low metastatic risk but high recurrence and local bone destruction; treat by excision or amputation, since radiation can cause high-grade transformation. A contradicts its low metastatic risk. C = BCC. D = melanoma. E is inadequate for a bone-invasive tumor.

9A 76-year-old retired farmer has an irregular brown-black macule on his left cheek that has slowly enlarged over 8 years. The surrounding skin shows marked solar damage. Biopsy shows atypical melanocytes along the basal layer of atrophic epidermis with focal dermal invasion. Which melanoma subtype is this?

D. Lentigo maligna melanoma: ~10% of melanomas, face (nose, cheek) of older patients with chronic sun exposure, slow growth; only ~5% of lentigo maligna in situ becomes invasive. A favors backs of men/legs of women. B is a rapid dark nodule. C is on palms, soles, nails. E lacks pigment.

10A 58-year-old Black man notes a dark streak in his right great toenail that has widened over a year. Exam shows a 6-mm irregular brown-black band, and pigment extends onto the proximal nail fold. He recalls no trauma. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

E. Periungual extension (Hutchinson sign) of a widening band = subungual acral lentiginous melanoma, the most common melanoma in skin of color (up to 70%), not UV-related and often diagnosed late. A grows out distally and spares the fold. B is uniform, often multiple, confined to the nail plate. C and D are not periungual tumors.

11A 47-year-old woman has a pigmented lesion excised from her calf. Pathology: superficial spreading melanoma, Breslow thickness 1.5 mm, no ulceration, margins narrow but clear. Imaging shows no distant disease. What is the most appropriate next step?

C. A 1.5-mm melanoma (T2a) needs wide excision with 1–2 cm margins plus SLNB (indicated from T1b; ~20% of melanomas >1 mm have nodal disease). A and B under-treat. D is not primary therapy. E is a BCC drug.

12Two patients each have a newly excised primary cutaneous melanoma without nodal or distant spread. Which pathologic feature is the single best predictor of which patient is more likely to die of the disease?

B. Breslow thickness is the #1 prognostic factor and the basis of T staging (with ulceration). A and C are screening clues (ABCDE), not prognostic. D is the older Clark level, inferior to Breslow. E guides targeted therapy and is even found in benign nevi.

13A 39-year-old woman has more than 100 nevi, many of them atypical. Her mother and brother had melanoma, and her maternal grandfather died of pancreatic cancer. A germline mutation in which gene is most likely?

A. CDKN2A (p16/p14ARF) accounts for ~40% of familial melanoma and raises pancreatic cancer risk. B → uveal melanoma, mesothelioma, RCC. C → Gorlin (BCC). D is a pigmentation risk variant, not a high-penetrance pancreatic syndrome. E mutations are somatic, not familial.

14A dermatopathologist is reviewing an asymmetric pigmented lesion from the back of a 44-year-old man. Which histologic finding most strongly supports melanoma rather than a benign melanocytic nevus?

E. Pagetoid scatter — single atypical melanocytes migrating upward through the epidermis — is the hallmark melanoma feature, along with pleomorphism and many mitoses. A, B (maturation), C and D all favor a benign nevus.
